Ibn Kathir cites a report lifting error, forgetfulness and coercion. Alusi considers non-obligation correct because a heedless command brings no benefit; Kuranyolu calls it legitimate excuse."}, {"id": "6:68/q29/p2", "position": "An act may remain due even though a heedless person is not presently addressable.", "reasons": "Ibn Burhan contrasts jurists' remaining duty with theologians' denial of an inconceivable command. {"id": "6:68/q30", "question": "Who are the wrongdoing people?", "turns_on": "Whether they are specifically polytheists or all open deniers and mockers.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q30/p1", "position": "They are polytheists or idolaters in this setting.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Abbas, Suddi, Razi and Qurtubi identify them."}, {"id": "6:68/q30/p2", "position": "They are gatherings of unbelievers and immoral people who openly deny or mock revelation.", "reasons": "Saʿid and Suddi give this broader identification; Ibn Ashur points to polemicists in the clause and Tabatabaʾi extends the rationale."}, {"id": "6:68/q30/p3", "position": "In an inward reading they put their own qualities in God's place.", "reasons": "Qashani says this veils the divine."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q31", "question": "Why are they explicitly called wrongdoers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q31/p1", "position": "The noun marks denial and mockery as injustice rather than using a neutral pronoun.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says they put things out of place; Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi specify substituting denial for belief and mockery for reverence. {"id": "6:68/q32", "question": "What does the verse imply about dissimulation by religious authorities?", "turns_on": "Whether the prohibition rules out taqiyya altogether or only when no independent proof safeguards the ruling.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q32/p1", "position": "It refutes permission for prophets or imams to associate with sinners and endorse their views as taqiyya.", "reasons": "Jubbaʾi argues this against the Imamis; Nahhas and Qurtubi likewise use the verse against such claimed permission."}, {"id": "6:68/q32/p2", "position": "An imam may use taqiyya only where decisive independent proof preserves the duty; prophets may omit repeating a ruling already explained.", "reasons": "Tabrisi rejects Jubbaʾi's accusation, says rulings known only through an imam cannot be concealed, and cites the report that the Prophet answered ʿUmar's kalala question by saying the sword verse sufficed; the note mentions 9:5."}]}
{"id": "6:68/q33", "question": "What spiritual reflections are drawn from this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q33/p1", "position": "Conveyance is the Messenger's duty; realization of divine connection belongs to God's will, and the realized should not return to veiled company.", "reasons": "Qushayri says remembrance restores alertness; the pure are spared wrongdoers' Resurrection pains, divine stratagems break their delusion, guidance cannot be traded for error or Paradise for Hell, and no new purpose obstructs God's power. {"id": "6:68/q34", "question": "What wider account of Qur'anic guidance and reform accompanies these notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q34/p1", "position": "The Qur'an aims at individual, collective and civilizational reform through sound belief and reflective reading.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur describes moral purification, worship, social rules, shared welfare and correction of false belief, citing 11:101 and 38:29. {"id": "6:68/q35", "question": "What rhetorical discussions use this passage as an example?", "turns_on": "Whether eloquence rests in ease of sound or meaning and arrangement, and how brevity compares with expansion.", "positions": [{"id": "6:68/q35/p1", "position": "Eloquence includes meaning, construction, and appropriate brevity or expansion.", "reasons": "Jurjani disputes an account that ranks inimitability by smooth articulation alone, citing clarity, allusion, simile, omission, joining and order. {"id": "6:76/q01", "question": "How does the nightfall scene connect to the preceding account?", "turns_on": "Whether the fāʾ resumes the vision of the kingdom in 6:75 or Abraham's speech to his father in 6:74.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q01/p1", "position": "It elaborates God's showing Abraham the heavenly kingdom and the ensuing reasoning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes the fāʾ as linking a summary to its detail; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the star belongs to that kingdom and rejects a remote link across a parenthesis. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī places it after rejection of idols and God's showing of creation's dependence; Islāḥī says celestial obedience to divine law expands the preceding account."}, {"id": "6:76/q01/p2", "position": "It resumes Abraham's earlier speech to his father; 'Thus We showed' is parenthetical.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn and some investigators cited by al-Ālūsī take 6:75 as an intervening parenthesis; al-Samīn prefers this."}, {"id": "6:76/q01/p3", "position": "This episode is distinct from the vision of the kingdom.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the nightfall is a different story."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q02", "question": "What does جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ ٱلَّيْلُ mean, and what does its root suggest?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase stresses mere covering, the onset of darkness, or a figurative inner night.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q02/p1", "position": "Night covered or concealed Abraham and darkened over him.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Mujāz, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī and later authors give this core sense. Poems by Durayd, a Hudhalī, ʿUbayd, and an anonymous poet illustrate covering darkness. The root explains jinn hidden from sight, and the garden, fetus, madness, shield, grave or heart as concealed or concealing; al-Rāghib says the root means concealment from the senses. Ibn ʿĀshūr pictures darkness like a garment and infers Abraham was outdoors; al-Biqāʿī says the brief verb intensifies darkness and ʿalā pictures it falling over him."}, {"id": "6:76/q02/p2", "position": "It is the darkness of bodily nature in childhood and early youth.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī's inward reading treats night as the body-bound state before spiritual ascent."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q03", "question": "What verbal forms and syntactic construction underlie جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ?", "turns_on": "How the simple and derived verbs differ in transitivity, darkness, and eloquence.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q03/p1", "position": "Janna ʿalayhi describes darkness falling; jannahu describes covering without the extra sense of darkening.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj prefers janna ʿalayhi and ajannahu; al-Jishumī distinguishes janna ʿalayhi from jannahu. Al-Samīn says the best usage makes the simple form intransitive and derived form transitive, while allowing both as transitive; al-Rāghib distinguishes providing a cover from covering itself. Al-Ṭabarī notes dialects: Asad uses jannah al-layl, Tamīm ajannah and jannah; his preferred alif forms and al-Jishumī's preferred non-alif form differ. Akhfash cites poems and junūn/جن as verbal nouns; Qays/Tamīm forms for concealment and 2:235, 37:49 are parallels."}, {"id": "6:76/q03/p2", "position": "The verb جَنَّ can be transitive with an omitted object, the visible things covered by night.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn cites a poem about night covering water as evidence for the less usual transitive form."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q04", "question": "Where and under what circumstances did Abraham first see the star?", "turns_on": "The sources offer different cave, emergence, travel, and observational circumstances.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q04/p1", "position": "He emerged from a cave at night or sunset and then saw the star.", "reasons": "Muqātil puts it at month's end; al-Suddī places the emergence after sunset. Ibn Isḥāq and historians say he recognized a creator from creatures after leaving the cave. Some accounts say parents brought him out and he reasoned from animals; a variant has him see the star through the cave's opening or split rock. Ibn ʿAṭiyya's tale says he first became aware of the world then. These versions differ in details."}, {"id": "6:76/q04/p2", "position": "He was with his people observing the sky and arguing against their star worship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr infers a group from the later address yā qawm; he identifies Chaldean Sabians. {"id": "6:76/q05", "question": "What reports describe Abraham's birth, concealment, and age at this episode?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on cave or riverbed, care, duration of concealment, and age.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q05/p1", "position": "Nimrod's astrologers forecast a boy who would change religion and topple or kill him, prompting an order to kill newborn boys.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says astrology and divination dominated; al-Thaʿlabī adds Nimrod ibn Canaan as first crown-wearer and a forecast said to be in prophetic books. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī recount watching pregnant women and killing boys; Ibn Isḥāq relates the warning."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p2", "position": "His mother concealed his birth in a cave and left him hidden there.", "reasons": "Versions have a cave birth while his father was away; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he sucked fingers that yielded honey and butter, while another says an angel fed him, or his mother brought milk from bereaved women. Al-Rāzī says Gabriel's miraculous care is possible, disputing the Qāḍī's objection to pre-mission marvels; his school allows irhāṣ. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ālūsī preserve the cave tradition."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p3", "position": "As a child he questioned his parents and Nimrod about their makers.", "reasons": "One account has the adults silence him; another has his mother call herself his lord, then his father and Nimrod, and rebuke dangerous questions. Ibn al-Jawzī's report places the parents' conversation inside the hiding place."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p4", "position": "He remained hidden or argued at seventeen years.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī lists seventeen cave years; al-Qurṭubī says he was seventeen when he argued with Nimrod; Bursevī repeats a seventeen-year cave account."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p5", "position": "He remained hidden for seven years.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī lists seven among three cave durations; al-Qurṭubī separately gives his age as seven."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p6", "position": "He remained hidden or reached the event at thirteen years.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and Bursevī record thirteen cave years, with Bursevī's Persian account saying he looked eighteen at eighteen months."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p7", "position": "He remained hidden for fifteen years, or was fifteen years old.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives ten or fifteen hidden years and Ibn Isḥāq, cited by al-Qurṭubī, gives fifteen as his age; the former also notes unusually fast growth."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p8", "position": "His mother hid him in a dry riverbed among reeds; his father made a sealed tunnel there.", "reasons": "The Ibn ʿAbbās report through Abū Ṣāliḥ says his mother nursed him in that tunnel."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p9", "position": "He remained hidden for ten years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives ten as an alternative to fifteen, with unusually fast growth."}, {"id": "6:76/q05/p10", "position": "He appeared mature at eighteen months, resembling an eighteen-year-old.", "reasons": "Bursevī transmits this Persian account, and reports how a relative revealed him to Āzar, who admired his beauty and was told to bring him to Nimrod."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q06", "question": "What is the star identified as?", "turns_on": "The transmitted identifications are Venus and Jupiter; some keep the star indefinite.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q06/p1", "position": "Venus.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to Zayd b. ʿAlī, Qatādah, Ibn ʿAbbās or Mujāhid; Muqātil places it near month's end. Several authors transmit Venus as one of two alternatives, and Islāḥī allows Venus or another star."}, {"id": "6:76/q06/p2", "position": "Jupiter.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to al-Suddī, Mujāhid or Ibn ʿAbbās; reports say it appeared at sunset toward the direction of prayer, and the moon rose late in the month."}, {"id": "6:76/q06/p3", "position": "No specific star is intended; the argument works for any setting star.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the indefinite noun deliberately avoids a particular identity and does not mean an arbitrary pointing at one of countless stars."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q07", "question": "What does كَوْكَبًا mean and how is it formed?", "turns_on": "The lexicographers differ over whether the initial kāf or wāw belongs to the root.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q07/p1", "position": "It is a star or shining celestial light.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān notes a broader sense for something shining with fire; Ibn Kathīr gives the ordinary gloss."}, {"id": "6:76/q07/p2", "position": "It is quadriliteral, with original wāw.", "reasons": "Al-Jawharī, perhaps following al-Layth, lists it as kawkab. Al-Samīn also reports an analysis as a rare repeated-radical quadriliteral on faʿfal, like fawfal."}, {"id": "6:76/q07/p3", "position": "The initial kāf is augmentative, so the root is wāw-kāf-bāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Ṣāghānī proposes this. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn dispute the alleged precedent Hindakī: the plural hanādik may be a longer paired form; Abū Ḥayyān instead takes Hindakī as an Ethiopian-derived nisba and denies that precise grammarians admit initial added kāf."}, {"id": "6:76/q07/p4", "position": "The word derives from k-b/b-k-b, with an extra wāw and substitution.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib proposes derivation from kabba and kabkaba; al-Samīn calls it very strange."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q08", "question": "How is رَءَا pronounced in the variant readings, and why?", "turns_on": "Full opening, full or partial imāla, and mixed vowel treatments depend on transmitted route and whether the following alif remains pronounced.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q08/p1", "position": "Both rāʾ and hamza are inclined toward kasra by imāla.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf appear in transmissions, with contextual differences. Imāla starts with original yāʾ and spreads to hamza and neighboring rāʾ; Abū ʿAmr also has a transmitted both-kasra route. Al-Fārisī adduces the imperfect pattern and guttural hamza for rāʾ kasra. Al-Wāḥidī says a dropped alif can remain conceptually present; al-Samīn details additional routes."}, {"id": "6:76/q08/p2", "position": "The rāʾ is open and hamza is inclined or kasra-marked.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr and Warsh from Nāfiʿ are named. Al-Fārisī says Nāfiʿ's intermediate form may incline only hamza or both vowels; Ibn Khālawayh's bayna-bayna lies between dialectal pronunciations."}, {"id": "6:76/q08/p3", "position": "Both rāʾ and hamza are open (fatḥa), without imāla.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim are named; other readers use this in the stated contexts. Al-Fārisī says the original form preserves alif from yāʾ after fatḥa, as with raʿā and ramā; al-Wāḥidī says the loss of the following alif removes the cause of imāla. Ibn Khālawayh prefers tafkhīm before alif-lām because the yāʾ disappears in pronunciation."}, {"id": "6:76/q08/p4", "position": "The rāʾ is kasra-marked while the hamza stays open.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports this for Ḥamza and Abū Bakr in a route, explaining rāʾ independently from hamza imāla; Ibn Khālawayh calls one report weak. Jishumī records this before a connecting alif, and Ibn al-Jawzī notes contexts before vowelless letters or attached pronouns."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q09", "question": "How does the first فَلَمَّا clause work syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether its answer is 'he saw' or 'he said,' and whether the speech is an independent sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q09/p1", "position": "'He saw a star' answers 'when night covered him'; 'he said' begins a new explanatory sentence.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān calls this the apparent parse; al-Samīn prefers independent speech, rejecting an adjective of kawkaban for lack of a linking pronoun and because the star would wrongly be made to speak. {"id": "6:76/q11", "question": "How should Abraham's words 'This is my Lord' be understood?", "turns_on": "Whether it is genuine inquiry or worship, a provisional hypothesis, a concession to opponents, an omitted quotation or question, or sarcasm; prophetic protection and the passage's sequence are decisive grounds in the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q11/p1", "position": "He stages or concedes his opponents' claim to refute it when the star sets.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba likens the method to a convert who feigned idol devotion; the tactic gains trust without provoking inherited beliefs. Al-Rāzī prefers it as a debater's fair rehearsal of a premise and cites 6:83; al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī prefer its gentle persuasion. Al-Ālūsī compares permitted speech under coercion and 37:88–89; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares faithful-hearted forced denial, says literal speech to a group and possible revelation made this strategy apt. Islāḥī calls it gradual argument, audible self-talk, double meaning and humor; ʿAbd Allāh b. Muslim and al-Farrāʾ are named as supporters. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows a hypothetical premise without asserting belief. The people's star worship, astrology, and assigned idols supply the audience."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p2", "position": "It is a rebuking question, 'Is this my Lord?', with the interrogative hamza omitted.", "reasons": "Poems cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī and 90:11 or 21:34 cited by later authors illustrate the omission. Ibn al-Anbārī calls it anomalous unless a cue such as am distinguishes the question; Ibn ʿAṭiyya disputes one poetic proof. The tone could signal the question, says al-Nasafī; Burhān states it directly."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p3", "position": "He actually believed or worshipped the star until it set.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports worship of each celestial body and subsequent disavowal; some take the plea for guidance as uncertainty. Opponents reject this for prophetic protection, 37:84's sound heart, prior guidance in 21:51, his dispute with his father in 6:74, 6:75's kingdom, and 6:83's public proof. Ibn Kathīr cites the fitra report; al-Rāzī argues even simple reason sees signs of creation. Abū Ḥayyān questions the Ibn ʿAbbās report's authenticity. The literal account is sometimes confined to childhood before accountability."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p4", "position": "He speaks according to his people's claim: 'this is my lord, as you say.'", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj compares God's ironic 'Where are My partners?' in 28:62; al-Wāḥidī adds 44:49. This treats the statement as attribution rather than Abraham's own belief."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p5", "position": "It is provisional inquiry or supposition, abandoned after testing.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Bayḍāwī allow reasoning from a hypothesis; al-Ṭabrisī says supposing eternity to expose absurdity need not be a false assertion, or it may report a thought provisionally entertained. Al-Ṭabarī, as cited by Ibn Kathīr, favors contemplation from the plea for guidance. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites Imams saying a seeker before conclusive proof did not commit shirk, and distinguishes later speakers. Al-Naḥḥās calls Abraham's progress 'light upon light': heart and signs preceded greater revealed knowledge. Al-Qurṭubī reports a mistaken identification of the star's light with the Lord's light."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p6", "position": "He spoke as a child before proof or legal responsibility, so the words were neither faith nor unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Baghawī and al-Qurṭubī report this; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says many place it before puberty. Al-Rāzī reports rigorous scholars' rejection of a post-puberty searching account; al-Ālūsī rejects the childhood-ignorance defense outright and says the context supports later mature debate."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p7", "position": "An omitted 'they say' or 'you say' makes the words a quotation.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and al-Rāzī cite elided speech elsewhere, especially the prayer after building the House in 2:127 and 39:3."}, {"id": "6:76/q11/p8", "position": "He said it ironically or sarcastically to taunt the claim.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares calling a lowly leader 'your master'; al-Ālūsī records the same alternative. Elmalılı says the words taunt onlookers about whether a star can nurture a human."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q12", "question": "What did Abraham's people worship, and why address stars?", "turns_on": "The sources differ in how idols, planets, and a supreme creator related in his people's worship.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q12/p1", "position": "They worshipped idols together with celestial bodies and sometimes Nimrod.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba describes an astrological culture claiming stars forecast hidden events; al-Zajjāj, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and Bursevī name sun, moon, stars and idols. Bursevī says some also worshipped Nimrod; Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies Chaldean Sabians and suggests planetary spirits, images or lesser idols. Kur'an Yolu dates Abraham around 2100 BCE and reports Torah/Ur tablets with about five thousand divine names."}, {"id": "6:76/q12/p2", "position": "They revered planets as delegated subordinate lords or governors.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says astrologers allowed the supreme deity to create planets which create lower plants and animals. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Sabians accepted the ultimate Creator but attributed earthly and human governance to celestial agents, explaining why arguments merely proving a first cause miss them; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows planets represented by images."}, {"id": "6:76/q12/p3", "position": "Celestial images were linked to planets, but the planets may have been thought independently effective.", "reasons": "An al-Ālūsī report assigns gold idols to the sun and silver to the moon, and says Abraham first denied images then their celestial sources."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q13", "question": "What does أَفَلَ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether disappearance specifically means horizon setting, a broader going away, or motion from the zenith.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q13/p1", "position": "It set or disappeared from view.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Isḥāq, Saʿīd b. {"id": "6:76/q14", "question": "What is meant by 'I do not love those that set'?", "turns_on": "Whether love is ordinary affection, refusal of worship, or the necessary bond between dependent creature and lord.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q14/p1", "position": "He refuses to take a disappearing being as a lord or object of worship.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī allows ordinary affection for stars; the rejected love is devotion to a worshipped lord. {"id": "6:76/q16", "question": "Why is setting, rather than rising, chosen as Abraham's test?", "turns_on": "Whether its force is clearer visible diminishment, the absence of oversight or love, or narrative economy.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q16/p1", "position": "Setting visibly removes light, apparent power and authority, making the proof clearer to ordinary hearers.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says motion at rising also shows origination, but its proof is subtle; al-Biqāʿī says rising retains honor and apparent authority, while setting displays insignificance. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Kashshāf emphasize concealment; al-Rāzī and al-Biqāʿī cite astrologers' view that planets weaken in the west. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports these readings but says they miss the verse's argument from love."}, {"id": "6:76/q16/p2", "position": "Setting makes the lord absent from dependents or unable to command enduring love.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says a continuously governing deity must attend servants' needs; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says only setting frustrates the love essential to lordship and rising is irrelevant to that direct proof."}, {"id": "6:76/q16/p3", "position": "The first setting of that day was not witnessed, so citing the observed setting is briefer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says using rising would require explaining that the star had set earlier."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q17", "question": "What exactly does the star's setting prove against lordship?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish change and origination, contingency, loss of presence, and love; some dispute whether first-cause arguments answer subordinate star worship.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q17/p1", "position": "A setting body changes, moves, is originated and governed, so cannot be a god.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj compares its states to acknowledged non-gods; al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr and others infer a creator or governor from movement and change. Qatādah contrasts it with an enduring Lord. Al-Rāzī says origination entails an eternal powerful agent or infinite regress, and the Creator of greater heavens can create humans without planet intermediaries (40:57, 36:81). Al-Biqāʿī says visible celestial bodies outrank earthly idols, so their failure also refutes idols; Elmalılı applies this to their fashioned images. Islāḥī says regulated celestial paths show subjection."}, {"id": "6:76/q17/p2", "position": "It reveals contingency and dependence on a Necessary Existent.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī assigns this to elite hearers and cites 53:42; Ibn Sīnā and al-Ghazālī treat the luminaries' possibility as requiring an efficient cause and necessary terminus. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it is an inference from setting, not the word's definition, yet argues star worshippers already accept dependent planets, so it misses their claim; al-Rāzī finds Ghazālī's reading possible but unlikely from the wording."}, {"id": "6:76/q17/p3", "position": "The same phrase teaches different audiences through contingency, motion, or visible loss of power.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Biqāʿī distinguish elite, intermediate, and ordinary hearers; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes each tier and rejects the layered proof as unsupported by the verse and ineffective against subordinate star worship."}, {"id": "6:76/q17/p4", "position": "It disproves a planet's continuous delegated governance because absence breaks its relation to those it governs.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the star's disappearance prevents attending dependents' needs and insists a change-based argument would not convince people who accept periodic celestial motion. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the dispute is over earthly governance, not a first creator; lack of durable beauty means lack of the love lordship requires, while mere invisibility alone would not prove it, since God is unseen."}, {"id": "6:76/q17/p5", "position": "The conclusion also forms a syllogism: the body sets; the true Lord does not.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī calls it a second-figure syllogism and, in this discussion, glosses the celestial body as the moon; al-Rāzī notes the Qur'an states foundational premises while dialectic expands them."}, {"id": "6:76/q17/p6", "position": "Setting is merely a popular insinuation that hidden stars do not know worshippers' affairs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this view but rejects it because the certainty and kingdom passages demand a demonstrative argument based on love rather than disappearance alone."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q18", "question": "What did Abraham know of God before and during this argument?", "turns_on": "Whether he was already certain, gained increasing knowledge, or was still seeking before conclusive proof.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q18/p1", "position": "He already knew God and had been protected from shirk; the scene argues to others.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba invokes the sound heart in 37:84, prior kingdom vision in 6:75, and earlier confrontation with his father. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī and others cite prophetic protection, 21:51, 6:83 and 14:35. Al-Rāzī says preaching his father gently preceded strong public polemic. Ibn Kathīr cites the newborn fitra report. Islāḥī argues this happened after appointment because prophets invite kin first and 6:79–80 speaks with authority; he calls the cave tale an invention to explain the order of luminaries. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī has Abraham know the supreme God even while examining proposed delegated governors."}, {"id": "6:76/q18/p2", "position": "He knew God by heart and signs, then received an increase of certain knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās's light-upon-light explanation, favored by al-Naḥḥās and quoted by al-Qurṭubī, relates 24:35 to Abraham; al-Naḥḥās cites 6:80. Islāḥī also calls prophetic revelation light upon light."}, {"id": "6:76/q18/p3", "position": "He was seeking his Lord without having reached disbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, as cited by Ibn Kathīr, bases contemplation on Abraham's request for guidance; Muqātil describes the same sequence. Reports from two Imams and al-Ṣādiq say his words while seeking were not shirk, though the same words from another after clear proof would be."}, {"id": "6:76/q18/p4", "position": "Some place the investigation after puberty and legal accountability.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this from a group and says al-Ṭabarī transmits it; al-Rāzī says rigorous scholars reject a post-puberty search for God."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q19", "question": "What does this episode teach about reasoning and religious knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is proof against imitation, inference from creation, or how to persuade an audience.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q19/p1", "position": "Faith and worship should rest on examination of created signs and proof, not imitation.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says prophetic knowledge is inferential, drawn from creatures, and that proof is necessary or Abraham's debate would be purposeless; al-Biqāʿī agrees. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the argument demonstrative and says the visible phenomena offered evidence suited to the conversation. Islāḥī says using innate intellect lifts heavenly bodies above man-made idols, while Kur'an Yolu says the sequence demonstrates correct belief and opposes associationism."}, {"id": "6:76/q19/p2", "position": "A preacher may use gradual, fair and indirect reasoning adapted to hostile listeners.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba's ḥawārī example, al-Nasafī's fair-minded rehearsal and al-Ālūsī's concern about obstinacy illustrate this. Islāḥī contrasts prophetic styles and says Abraham's adversarial audience required staged reasoning, possible turiya, humor and sarcasm; his idol-smashing argument elicited their own admission that idols cannot speak."}, {"id": "6:76/q19/p3", "position": "The higher Creator can dispense with all celestial intermediaries.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says if stars created humans no one could identify which to thank, while the one creator of everything is knowable and deserves worship."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q20", "question": "How does Abraham's example function in this sūra and for Muhammad's audience?", "turns_on": "The notes relate his universal reputation, prophetic continuity, and the sūra's argument against associationism.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q20/p1", "position": "Its anti-idolatry reasoning turns from earthly idols to more impressive celestial bodies.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Biqāʿī and Elmalılı say if visible, brighter heavenly objects fail the test, handmade idols fail more clearly. {"id": "6:76/q22", "question": "How do cited poems use moon and sun imagery?", "turns_on": "Whether definiteness and number imply literal luminaries or figurative human counterparts.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q22/p1", "position": "Definite 'the moon' tends toward the actual moon; plural moons or 'I am a sun' admit a human metaphor.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says al-Mutanabbī's 'two moons at once' pairs the real moon with a woman's sun-like face; two compared poems choose day or night but have the same poetic substance, and Abū al-Fatḥ captured only the general image of a gazelle and sunlight, not its special craft."}, {"id": "6:76/q22/p2", "position": "The word qamar names the familiar moon and evokes whiteness.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, as cited by Abū Ḥayyān, relates it to a bright qamrāʾ night."}]}

{"id": "6:76/q24", "question": "What other reports or objections are attached to this story?", "turns_on": "These are separate transmitted applications or doubts about the narrative's setting.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q24/p1", "position": "A report about seeing sins in the kingdom says God restrained Abraham's imprecations.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports that a sinner may repent, bear good offspring, or face the Fire."}, {"id": "6:76/q24/p2", "position": "The Prophet's east-and-west report is connected to Abraham's rejection of setting stars.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī says the source of fitna and disbelief is toward the east, while repentance's door opens from the west."}, {"id": "6:76/q24/p3", "position": "Harran poses a historical objection to the proposed timing of the debate.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī admits that Abraham could only have debated celestial worshippers after reaching Harran, so his earlier interpretation of the passage faces a problem."}, {"id": "6:76/q24/p4", "position": "The daytime absence of the sun from the opening scene has several possible explanations.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests the family debate left no time before night, clouds obscured the sun, or the people were present only at sunrise."}]}
{"id": "6:76/q25", "question": "What is the 'kingdom' shown to Abraham in the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q25/p1", "position": "It means the signs.", "reasons": "Mujāhid gives this gloss of malakūt, supplying the context for the sight of the star."}]}

{"id": "6:76/q28", "question": "What further evidence and objections bear on Abraham's wording and argument?", "turns_on": "How contextual sequence and analogy are used to assess the narrative.", "positions": [{"id": "6:76/q28/p1", "position": "A quoted ironic address can describe how claimants see themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites the address 'You are indeed the mighty and noble' in 44:49 as an analogy for attributed speech."}, {"id": "6:76/q28/p2", "position": "A supposedly first observed setting raises an objection because the luminaries had set before.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports an objector's question about what this particular night adds; his reply puts the emphasis on demonstrating the loss of power before star worshippers."}, {"id": "6:76/q28/p3", "position": "Accounts of a debate after maturity are challenged on contextual grounds.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects the proposed settings of that mature public debate, especially the Imam's, because they rely on the very mature-mission sequence they invoke."}, {"id": "6:76/q28/p4", "position": "The sequence may have taken about two days and one night.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī estimates this duration for the family and celestial debates."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q01", "question": "How is رَءَا read here?", "turns_on": "The vowel treatment of rāʾ, hamza and the underlying alif, with differences by reader, transmission and following sound.", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q01/p1", "position": "Both rāʾ and hamza are opened.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī lists Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn ʿĀmir before a consonant and Ḥafṣ throughout; Jishumī calls this the reading of the remaining readers. Al-Fārisī compares 18:53 and 16:86 and says opening can follow ramā and raʿā or preserve a second accepted language form."}, {"id": "6:77/q01/p2", "position": "The rāʾ is inclined or broken while the hamza is opened.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī attributes it to Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza, and permits independent kasra of rāʾ without hamza imāla. Al-Fārisī rejects calling the hamza a literal kasra: its fatḥa is inclined."}, {"id": "6:77/q01/p4", "position": "The rāʾ is opened and the hamza inclined or broken.", "reasons": "Jishumī attributes this throughout to Abū ʿAmr and Warsh from Nāfiʿ. {"id": "6:77/q03", "question": "What does ٱلْقَمَرَ mean and why is it so named?", "turns_on": "Competing reported explanations of the noun's derivation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q03/p1", "position": "Qamar is the moon after its first three nights, named for its whiteness or spreading light.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Ṭabrisī call the first three nights hilāl and the remainder qamar; Ibn al-Jawzī transmits Ibn Qutayba's aqmar 'white' and layla qamrāʾ 'bright night.' {"id": "6:77/q04", "question": "What does بَازِغًۭا mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q04/p1", "position": "Rising or first appearing, with light breaking through darkness.", "reasons": "Majāz, Ṭabarī, Māwardī, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, Ibn Kathīr, Biqāʿī and Ālūsī give rising, first appearance or spreading light; some apply it also to sun and stars. Al-Azharī derives it from splitting darkness; Wāḥidī cites al-Ṭirimmāḥ's veterinary incision, while Jishumī, Qurṭubī, Samīn and Ālūsī add bloodletting or tooth emergence as cognate uses."}]}
{"id": "6:77/q05", "question": "What is the grammatical role of بَازِغًۭا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:77/q05/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative describing the moon.", "reasons": "Samīn says the root verb can be transitive of a veterinarian releasing blood or intransitive of blood flowing, before its generalized use for rising."}]}
